result:
There's a moment, maybe the third or fourth time you're reading a single word, where the ink on the page goes flat. The word "because" just looks like a shape. A squiggle. You've been staring at it for three seconds and now it's not a word at all. It's just four letters you know how to draw. And you feel this tiny, almost absurd panic, the way your name does when someone says it in a strange voice or you catch yourself in a mirror on a bad morning — the self goes briefly, politely, out of the room.

Then it snaps back. *Because.* Of course. You connect two thoughts. You keep reading.

It happens to me every day, and no one else knows to expect it. I'm sitting at a desk and the whole machinery of language just... stutters. And I realize it's not that the word is hard. It's that it's become so transparent, so worn smooth by repetition, that my brain forgot to do the one thing it does for free: render the word into a little warm packet of meaning, the way a hand remembers the weight of a stone without actually thinking about its density. And then the packet reforms, slightly warm, and I'm back in the sentence.

I wonder if other people feel that tiny flicker. I probably don't. I probably just reread the line and move on, never noticing the two seconds where "because" was just a drawing. And maybe that's the whole secret: meaning isn't a thing. It's a small, repeated act of attention, and some mornings it's so easy it disappears entirely.
